# Caching

[Section](README.md) · [System design](../README.md) · [Home](../../README.md)

> **In one line:** keep hot data closer to the reader. Every caching decision is a trade between freshness and latency.

## Notes

- **Layers:** browser → CDN → reverse proxy → application (in-process) → distributed cache (Redis/Memcached) → database buffer pool.
- **Hit ratio** is what matters: a 99% hit ratio means the database sees 1% of reads. Size the cache for the working set, not the whole data set.
- **Eviction:** LRU (the default), LFU (stable popularity), TTL (time-bounded staleness).
- **Problems to name in interviews:** the *thundering herd* or cache stampede (many misses at once: fix with request coalescing or locks and jittered TTLs), *hot keys* (fix with local caches or replicated keys), *cold start* (fix with warming).

## Trade-offs

| Strategy | Pros | Cons | Use when |
|---|---|---|---|
| Cache-aside (lazy) | Only caches what is read; the cache can fail open | First read is a miss; stale until TTL or invalidation | General default for reads |
| Read-through | App code is simpler | The cache library must know the DB | Managed caches |
| Write-through | Cache always fresh | Write latency is higher; caches unread data | Read-after-write consistency matters |
| Write-back (write-behind) | Fast writes, batching | Data loss if the cache dies before flushing | Counters, analytics |
| Write-around | Avoids caching write-once data | Next read misses | Logs, bulk loads |

## Flashcards

The whole note is reviewed as one item: answer each card out loud before opening it, then log the review with `prep stop`.

<details><summary>Q: What is a cache stampede and two ways to prevent it?</summary>

A: Many requests miss the same expired key at once and all hit the database. Prevent it with request coalescing or a mutex (one request rebuilds the value, the rest wait), jittered or early probabilistic expiry, or serving stale data while revalidating.

</details>

<details><summary>Q: Cache-aside read and write flow?</summary>

A: Read: check the cache, on a miss read the DB and populate the cache. Write: update the DB, then **delete** the cache key (not update it) to avoid racing writers leaving stale data.

</details>

<details><summary>Q: Why delete instead of update the cache on write?</summary>

A: Two concurrent writers can update the DB in one order and the cache in the other, leaving the cache permanently stale. Deleting makes the next reader fetch the committed value.

</details>

<details><summary>Q: LRU vs LFU?</summary>

A: LRU evicts the least recently used item: simple, adapts fast, but one scan can flush the cache. LFU evicts the least frequently used: protects stable hot items but adapts slowly to shifting popularity.

</details>

<details><summary>Q: When would you NOT add a cache?</summary>

A: Write-heavy data with few repeat reads, data that must be strictly consistent (balances), or when the DB already meets latency targets. A cache adds a consistency problem and an extra failure mode.

</details>
